summary: Black rice fritters with roasted turnips and horseradish cream: cooked black rice bound with eggs and toasted caraway and pan-fried about 2 minutes per side, served with baby turnips roasted at 450°F then seared, a reduced cream sauce with fresh horseradish and whole grain mustard; serves 4.
glance: 3 cups cooked black rice (about 1 1/2 cups raw)
1/3 cup patted to no more than 1/2 inch, about 2 minutes per side
12 baby turnips roasted at 450°F until very tender, then seared in butter
faq: Why caraway, horseradish and mustard with black rice?

Black rice reminded the author, obliquely, of pumpernickel, which inspired a favorite set of Eastern European flavors: caraway, horseradish and mustard, a natural fit with baby turnips from the farmer's market.
What black rice should I use?
The author used Hinode black rice, which is longer grain than the "forbidden rice" you may know, though that works ok too. Red rice or even brown rice would be okay but not as visually dramatic.
How do I make the horseradish cream?

Simmer minced onion, 2 cups heavy cream, salt and grated fresh horseradish (or prepared) until the cream coats the back of a spoon and you can drag a finger through the coating and leave a clean line, then strain. Taste and adjust: the horseradish should be present but not overpowering.
How do I cook the turnips?

Roast baby turnips (stems attached) at 450°F until very tender and easily pierced, then halve and sear in butter until golden. This roast-then-sear method works with many root vegetables, and can be done in the other order.
Why fritters?
In a vegetarian meal the grain can be thought of as the gravitational center of the plate; fritters define that center in a way other than the typical bed of rice or crust of bread.

summary: Caramel-cooked tofu: extra-firm tofu squares fried 4 minutes until golden, then flipped and glazed in the pan with a rice wine, soy, sesame, garlic, ginger and sugar sauce that caramelizes in about 4 more minutes; vegan, 20 minutes, serves 2-4.
glance: 2 hungry adults with rice, or 4 as part of a spread
about 4 minutes on the first side, then about 4 more in the sauce
1 pound extra-firm in 2 x 2 x 1/3-inch squares, patted thoroughly dry
Vegan and gluten-free (with gluten-free soy sauce)
faq: What is caramel cooking?

A Vietnamese technique most often applied to chicken that works equally well for deeply flavored tofu lacquered with a sweet, salty, fragrant sauce. Traditionally the caramel is made separately, but Chef John of Food Wishes devised this simpler way to make the sauce right in the pan.
How do I make the sauce?

Whisk together the rice wine, rice vinegar, soy sauce, sesame oil, garlic, ginger and sugar until the sugar dissolves. After flipping the browned tofu, pour it into the hot pan with the onions (and chile pods) where it splutters and caramelizes.
How do I keep from burning it?
Keep a close eye on it and move the tofu around a little so the sauce gets under it, cooking until the sauce thickens to a fairly thick glaze coating the tofu.
Can I add vegetables?

A small amount of vegetable: fresh bamboo shoots are excellent. Cook something that takes a few minutes, like broccoli, separately first and add it at the end; tender items such as red bell peppers can go in with the onion.
What do I serve with it?
Just rice, for two; or as part of a larger spread.

summary: Cucumber, radish and cilantro raita: 2 cups of thick plain yogurt beaten about a minute until smooth and creamy, then mixed with grated cucumber and radish, cilantro, salt and lemon juice to a thick but pourable consistency; serves at least 4 as a condiment.
glance: 2 cups plain, preferably thick Greek style, beaten about 1 minute first
1/2 to 1 cucumber, 6 radishes, cilantro, 1 teaspoon salt, 1 tablespoon lemon juice
faq: What is raita?

A simple yogurt-based sauce served with almost any Indian meal: a cooling condiment when a curry is too spicy, and especially good mixed with basmati rice. The most common version uses grated cucumber, like Greek tzatziki.
Why beat the yogurt?

The yogurt should be thick and is always thoroughly beaten before mixing in the garnish (about 1 minute, until you see the texture thin out). Beating makes it smooth and creamy and more appealing as a sauce.
What variations exist?
The possibilities are endless: banana raita, spicy raita, eggplant raita, even vermicelli raita. This version could take roasted cumin seeds, black pepper and fresh mint.
How thick should it be?
Thick but liquid and pourable; add a tablespoon of water at a time if needed.
Which yogurt is best?
The author prefers thicker Greek styles such as Fage, Greek Gods or Oikos.

summary: Polenta with sauteed chard and gorgonzola: polenta made Marcella Hazan's low-maintenance way (stirred a minute every ten minutes over 40 minutes, then 5 more) with Parmesan, topped with garlicky steamed Swiss chard, gorgonzola dolce and optional balsamico; serves 4.
glance: 1 2/3 cups medium to coarse polenta in 7 cups water; 40 minutes covered plus 5 uncovered
1 large bunch, sauteed with garlic then steamed about 7 minutes
Vegetarian and gluten-free; vegan if you omit the cheese
faq: What is Marcella Hazan's "no-stir" polenta?

It isn't really no-stir but definitely low maintenance: whisk the polenta into boiling salted water in a thin stream, stir 2 minutes, reduce to a simmer and cover; every ten minutes uncover and stir a full minute, and re-cover until 40 minutes have elapsed, then cook uncovered 5 more and stir in Parmesan. It takes about an hour.
How does it differ from quick-cooking polenta?

Both make delicious polenta but they are very different: the quick-cooking de la Estancia is bright yellow and tastes of fresh corn with a slightly rougher texture, while Hazan's method yields polenta that is very mellow, creamy, soft and soothing.
What do I do with leftover polenta?
The author almost always doubles the batch and chills the rest on an oiled baking sheet; the next day he cuts it into squares and fries it in a skillet, delicious with a simple tomato sauce.
How much blue cheese should I use?
The polenta is the main event so strong flavors should be moderate. The author thinks the amount of blue cheese in the photo is too much by half; the recipe uses 6 tablespoons for four.
How do I cook the chard?

Fry sliced garlic (and optional chili flakes) 10 seconds, add chopped chard and salt, saute a minute, add a little water, cover and steam about 7 minutes until thoroughly tender, then remove the lid to evaporate the water.

summary: Zabaglione with roasted plums: egg yolks, sugar, plum brandy and water whisked over a double boiler 5 to 10 minutes into a fluffy custard, chilled and spooned over Italian plums roasted 15 minutes at 400°F; serves 4 in 20 minutes plus cooling.
glance: 12 Italian plums, halved, roasted at 400°F about 15 minutes with 2 tablespoons sugar
4 egg yolks, 1/4 cup sugar, 1/4 cup plum brandy plus 1/4 cup water (or 1/2 cup Marsala)
faq: What is zabaglione?
Similar to custard but made with only egg yolks, sugar and flavoring, with no milk or cream. The yolks are whisked over a double boiler and incorporate a lot of air, becoming creamy, rich and fluffy.
What spirit should I use?

Traditionally Marsala wine. The author prefers a spirit made from the same fruit as the one served, such as plum brandy (slivovitz, popular in the Balkans), like the one from Oregon's Clear Creek Distillery. If you can't find a plum spirit, use another fruit spirit, grappa or Marsala.
How do I keep the yolks from scrambling?

Whisk continuously over barely simmering water. If you sense the yolks are at risk of scrambling, quickly remove from the heat and whisk to cool slightly, then continue. It's done when soft peaks form, about 5 to 10 minutes.
What fruit can I use besides plums?
Italian plums are small, oval and firm enough to stand a little cooking, but peaches, pears or even apples also work.
Can I serve it without chilling?
If you don't have time to chill the zabaglione, it is perfectly appropriate to serve it at room temperature. Give it a quick whisk before spooning it over the plums.

summary: Sesame-flax soda bread: all-purpose and whole wheat flours, flax meal and toasted sesame seeds cut with cold butter, mixed with an egg and 2 cups of buttermilk, kneaded a couple of minutes and baked at 425°F for about 40 minutes until 180°F inside; about 10 minutes of work.
glance: 425°F for about 40 minutes, until golden, hollow-sounding, 180°F (83°C) inside
faq: What is soda bread?

A third option beyond buying artisan bread or making a yeast loaf: because the leavening is baking soda, you don't have to develop the gluten or the yeast, so it needs only a quick mixing and goes right in the oven. It's cakier than yeast bread, with its own kind of pleasure.
How do I work with whole grains?

Whole-grain breads have a coarser texture and distinct flavors; the key is to work with those flavors, not just substitute them blindly for white flour. This cakier bread wants butter, not olive oil, and pairs better with an onion-and-garlic soup than a smoked paprika one.
How do I know the bread is done?

Golden brown and sounds hollow when rapped on the bottom, or better, an internal temperature of 180°F/83°C on an instant-read thermometer. If it browns too fast after about 20 minutes, cover it with a tinfoil tent.
How do I store flax meal?
The author uses Bob's Red Mill. Once opened, seal the leftovers tightly in a plastic bag and freeze, because the oils go rancid quickly at room temperature.
How do I cut in the butter?
With two knives or a pastry cutter, as for pie crust. If your butter is frozen, microwave it 10 seconds at a time until it's cuttable.

summary: Spaghetti aglio e olio: 8 cloves of sliced garlic softened (not browned) about 3 minutes in olive oil with chile flakes and salt, then tossed over medium-high heat with spaghetti and about 1/2 cup of the starchy pasta water; ready two minutes after the pasta, serves 3-4.
glance: 8 cloves, softened about 3 minutes but not browned
reserve 1 cup; toss with 1/2 cup first
faq: Why is aglio e olio a good weeknight dish?

Other than noodles with butter and cheese, it's about the simplest way to eat pasta. You can have it ready two minutes after the pasta is done boiling, so it makes a perfect meal when the day gets away from you.
What are the technique points?

Cook the garlic gently until softened but not browned, turn off the heat until the pasta is ready, boil the spaghetti for the minimum time on the package and test for al dente, then toss the pasta in the oil over medium-high heat with some of the reserved starchy pasta water.
Should I add cheese and breadcrumbs?
The author often gilds the lily with Parmesan and fresh breadcrumbs, though some insist that's sacrilege. The choice is yours.
What makes it outstanding?
The clean, direct flavors of extra-virgin olive oil and garlic, spiked with a few chile flakes.
How do I keep it from being dry?
Add the pasta water a bit at a time, tossing thoroughly with tongs; add more of the reserved liquid if it seems dry.

summary: Spicy nori popcorn seasoning, a simple furikake: two nori sheets and a dried chili toasted about 20 seconds over an open flame, then ground to a fine powder with 1/2 teaspoon of sea salt in a spice grinder; about 5 minutes, enough for many batches of popcorn.
glance: enough for many, many servings of popcorn
2 nori sheets, 1 dried chili (morita is nice), 1/2 teaspoon sea salt
yield: enough for many servings of popcorn
faq: What is furikake?
A dry seasoning usually used on rice but delicious in many contexts; gomashio is another example. A good Japanese grocer sells many blends, some vegetarian and some not. This is a very simple one.
How do I toast the nori and chili?

Hold each nori sheet in tongs and toast lightly over an open medium flame for maybe 20 seconds, moving it around so the whole sheet toasts, being careful not to set it on fire or burn your hands. Do the same with the chili pepper.
Why grind it so fine?
Grinding very finely allows the seasoning to adhere to the popcorn. Whiz in a spice grinder for a long time until a completely fine powder.
How do I use it?
Sprinkle liberally on freshly popped corn, tossing to coat. After making it once you can adjust the salt, umami and heat ratio to your preference.
What else can I use it on?
The author mentions offering it on the side of a Japanese fusion veggie ceviche.

summary: Irish soda bread, adapted from Saveur: half pastry and half whole wheat flour with cold butter, buttermilk and an egg (with optional raisins, currants or caraway), kneaded a couple of minutes and baked at 425°F for about 40 minutes until 180°F inside; under an hour from start to table.
glance: under an hour, a few minutes of active work
425°F for about 40 minutes, until golden, hollow-sounding, 180°F inside
2 cups pastry flour and 2 cups whole wheat (any 4 cups of wheat flour works)
faq: Why make soda bread?

It's leavened with baking soda and buttermilk instead of yeast, so you can go from conception to hot bread on the table in under an hour with only a few minutes of active work. It's also fun to make with kids.
Can I change the flour?

Basically any four cups of wheat-based flour is fine. Pastry flour gives a more tender bread but all-purpose works, or you could use half all-purpose and half whole wheat pastry flour. The recipe adapts beautifully to half whole wheat to boost the nutritional value.
What can I add?
1 cup of raisins or currants, 1.5 tablespoons of caraway seeds, or nothing, to suit your mood or menu.
Why use real buttermilk?

The author likes keeping buttermilk as a staple: powdered buttermilk or milk-and-vinegar and yogurt substitutions can be good, but real buttermilk is more consistent and lasts quite a while in the fridge.
How do I know it's done?
Golden brown and hollow-sounding when rapped on the bottom, or better, an internal temperature of 180°F with an instant-read thermometer. If it browns too fast, cover it with a tinfoil tent.
